title: Curry Ketchup and Tandoori Naanwiches: India Storms America's Biggest Food Trade Show
excerpt: At this weekend's Summer Fancy Food Show in New York, Indian flavors were everywhere — and the industry's trend-spotters are calling it a mainstream moment.
body:
Inside the Jacob K. Javits Convention Center in New York this weekend, between the artisanal vinegars and the pumpkin salsas, a quiet revolution is on display. India has arrived at the Summer Fancy Food Show — and it is not playing small.

The 56th edition of North America's largest specialty food and beverage trade show, running June 28-30, has drawn 2,400 exhibitors from 80 countries showcasing 180,000 products. Among them, India's Agricultural and Processed Food Products Export Development Authority (APEDA) has set up a sprawling India Pavilion spanning roughly 3,500 square feet, with more than 30 exhibitor booths marketing Indian agricultural and processed food products to American buyers, distributors and restaurateurs.

But the real story is not the pavilion's size. It is what the show's own trend-spotters are saying. The National Association for the Specialty Food Trade's expert panel named "Indian products go mainstream" as one of the show's defining trends for 2026, alongside great vinegars and handcrafted heritage foods. Specific products flagged included curry ketchup, cashew-and-cream cooking sauces, tandoori chicken naanwiches and — in a phrase that would have been unthinkable a decade ago — tikka masala marinara.

## The New Guard

Two exhibitors in particular signal where India's packaged food ambitions are headed. Doosra, a producer of Indian-style snack mixes, showcased its modern chaats — a product called "The Mix" blends spiced boondi (crisp chickpea puffs), roasted peanuts and caramelized white chocolate into a sweet-savory snack designed for American palates without abandoning Indian identity. It is the kind of product that would be right at home in a Whole Foods aisle.

Arya, which bills itself as "a modern Indian kitchen," displayed rotis in four varieties — Cumin Spinach, Whole Wheat, Chia Multigrain and Golden Curry. The company recently won a sofi New Product Award for its Methi Roti, which incorporates turmeric and fenugreek leaf. Wrapped around a filling of dal or spiced potatoes, Arya pitches its rotis as the Indian answer to the wrap — quick, portable and genuinely authentic.

## The Numbers Behind the Trend

The timing is not coincidental. Indian food is now the second-fastest-growing global cuisine in America, according to Dataessential research. The U.S. ethnic food market is estimated at $24.5 billion, and Indian food's share is growing faster than almost any other category. Premium Indian brands — Gymkhana Fine Foods launched at Whole Foods this spring, and Truly Indian picked up two NEXTY Award finalist nods — are proving that there is consumer demand for Indian products that go beyond the jarred curry sauces of the 1990s.

The condiments category in particular is booming. The Fancy Food Show's organizers noted that condiments broke into the top 10 specialty food categories by growth for the first time this year. Tamarind — a staple of South Indian cooking that McCormick named its "flavor of the year" — is now appearing in barbecue sauces and chutneys from exhibitors who have nothing to do with India.

## What It Means for NRIs

For the Indian diaspora, the mainstreaming of desi flavors is bittersweet. On one hand, there is pride in seeing turmeric and tamarind treated with the same reverence as truffle oil and balsamic vinegar. On the other, there is a familiar anxiety about authenticity — will "tikka masala marinara" respect the cuisine's depth, or flatten it into another fusion gimmick?

The answer, increasingly, is both. And the best antidote to flattening is presence. With APEDA investing in a massive trade show pavilion, brands like Doosra and Arya designing products that are authentically Indian but commercially savvy, and the industry's gatekeepers naming Indian flavors as a top trend, the desi food ecosystem now has a seat at the table where American food trends are made.

The naanwich, it turns out, was just the beginning.
